units.translation: The scholiast: ἰσόπτερος [equal-winged], κούφη [light]. Hesychius: άπτερα [wingless things]: ἰσόπτερα [equal-winged], ταχέα [swift], ηδέα [pleasant]. The same: άπτερος [wingless]: αἰφνίδιος [sudden], in Homer. ὁ προσηνής [the gentle] or ταχύς [swift]. Aeschylus in the Agamemnon. [αἰφνίδιον [sudden].] The same: ἀπτέρωτα [wingless things]: ταχέα [swift], αἰφνίδια [sudden]. Etym. M. p. 133, 26. ἄπτερος [wingless]: “τῇ δ᾽ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μύθος” [and the word was wingless for her] (in Homer Od. 7, 57 and elsewhere) ταχὺς πρὸς τὸ πεισθῆναι [swift to be persuaded], and ἰσόπτερος [equal-winged], for the privative ἂ denotes both likeness and equality, as in ἀτάλαντος [equal in weight], ἄλοχος [sharing a bed]. But some say not παραπτάς [flying past], but ἔμμονος [abiding]. Others say ἄπτερον [wingless] means τὸ ἡδὺ [the sweet], ἄσμενον [welcome], ὀρθόν [right]. The observations of other grammarians on this word and on ἀπτερέως [without wings] are collected in Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 1831. Hermann correctly says: "Among the Attic tragedians, wherever ἄπτερος [wingless] is found, it sometimes means not winged in the proper sense, as in Eum. 51 250 and in Iph. Taur. 1095, sometimes unfledged, as in Here. fur. 1039 ὁ δ᾽, ὥς τις ὄρνις ἄπτερον καταστένων | ὠδῖνα τέκνων, πρέσβυς ὑστέρῳ ποδί | πικρὰν διώκων ἤλυσιν πάρεσθ᾽ ὅδε [and he, like a bird lamenting the unfledged brood of its young, an old man with halting foot pursuing a bitter journey, is here]. And this passage is most suitable for defending this word in the Agamemnon against Turnebus' conjecture εὔπτερος [well-winged]. For ἄπτερος φάτις [wingless report] is an untimely rumor, to which credence is not yet to be given, by a comparison taken from birds whose wings are not yet strengthened for flight. But it is not obscure that those who seem to have used that word in the opposite sense have in reality not departed from the proper one. For they followed Homer, for whom, since άπτερος μῦθος [wingless word] means not flying away, but carefully guarded in the mind, ἄπτερος [wingless], ἀπτέρως [without wings], ἀπτερέως [without wings] are said of things which are done not lightly or carelessly, but diligently and vigorously."
These at least are wingless to behold.
But did some wingless rumor charm you?
because of the homonymy with birds
wingless: sudden, in Homer. the gentle or swift. Aeschylus in the Agamemnon. [sudden]
wingless: “and the word was wingless for her”

swift to be persuaded, and equal-winged, for the privative a- denotes both likeness and equality, as in equal in weight, sharing a bed. But some say not flying past, but abiding. Others say wingless means the sweet, welcome, right.
and he, like a bird lamenting the unfledged brood of its young, an old man with halting foot pursuing a bitter journey, is here

ἀντὶ τοῦ ᾠῶν [instead of eggs]. τινὲς δὲ κελύφων [but some say shells], where it is used improperly in a verse which can be gathered from the gloss of Photius p. 353, 17 to be Aeschylus' (fr. 401): ὀστράκων: τῶν τοῦ ᾠοῦ [of shells: of the egg]. Αἰσχύλος [Aeschylus].
unfledged, tiny, just naked from the shell
instead of eggs. but some say shells
